chapters.title: Chapter 4: Convexity: Where Duration Falls Short

lessons.title: The Curve Duration Ignores: Why Linear Estimates Break Down

children.text: In the summer of 2013, the US Federal Reserve hinted at slowing its bond buying, foreign investors pulled money out of India, the rupee slid, and RBI tightened liquidity sharply. Within about three months, the 10-year G-Sec yield jumped roughly 200 basis points, from around 7.2% to above 9%. Moves like that are rare, but they are exactly when you most need an accurate estimate of what your bonds are worth. And they are exactly when duration, the tool you spent all of Chapter 3 mastering, starts to give the wrong answer. This chapter is about why, and how to fix it.

body.text: Duration draws a straight line through a relationship that is actually a curve. For small yield moves the line and the curve agree. For large moves they separate, and the gap between them is convexity.

children.text: A Straight Line Against a Curve

markDefs.definition: The curvature of a bond's price-yield relationship. It measures how much the bond's duration itself changes as yields change, and explains why duration-based price estimates drift for large yield moves.

children.text: Plot a bond's price against its yield and you do not get a straight line. You get a curve that bows towards the origin: steep on the left, where yields are low, and flatter on the right, where yields are high. Modified duration describes the slope of that curve at one point, today's yield. Using it to estimate price changes is like drawing a straight line that just touches the curve at today's yield and reading prices off the line instead of the curve. Near the touching point, you cannot tell them apart. Further away, the curve always sits above the line. That bend is

body.title: 30-Year 7% G-Sec: Actual Price vs Duration Line (₹ per ₹100 face value)

children.text: We use an illustrative 30-year G-Sec with a 7% coupon, priced at par at a 7% yield, because long bonds make the curve easy to see. Its modified duration is 12.47. At 7% the line and curve meet at ₹100. At 10%, the line says ₹62.58; the bond is actually worth ₹71.61. At 4%, the line says ₹137.42; the bond is actually worth ₹152.14. The line is wrong in both directions, and wrong in the same way: too low.

body.caption: 30-year 7% G-Sec at par (modified duration 12.47): duration estimate vs actual price change

body.title: How Much Duration Misses by, for Yield Rises of Different Sizes (%)

children.text: The error does not grow in proportion to the yield move. It grows roughly with its square. Double the move from 100 to 200 basis points and the error jumps from 1.16% to 4.31%, close to four times. Go from 50 to 300 basis points, six times the move, and the error grows about thirty times. That is why duration is superb for everyday moves of 5 to 25 basis points and increasingly unreliable for shocks like 2013.

body.title: Scale the error
body.prompt: For a bond, duration misses the actual price change by 0.30 percentage points when yields rise 50 basis points. Using the rule of thumb that the error roughly quadruples each time the yield move doubles, estimate the error for a 100 basis point rise.
body.explanation: Doubling the move from 50 to 100 bps multiplies the error by about 4: 0.30 × 4 = 1.2 percentage points. For the 30-year G-Sec in the table, the actual error at +100 bps is 1.16%, very close to the rule of thumb.

children.text: Why the Curve Bends: Duration Changes as Yields Move

Recall the third risk driver from Chapter 3: lower yields make a bond more sensitive, higher yields less. So duration is not a fixed property of a bond. As yields rise, the bond's duration shrinks, and each further rise hurts a little less than the one before. As yields fall, duration grows, and each further fall helps a little more. A single duration number, measured at today's yield, cannot capture this. Convexity does.

body.context: A duration measured at 7% overstates the risk once yields are higher and understates it once yields are lower.

body.title: Duration after a sell-off
body.question: Your 30-year G-Sec had a modified duration of 12.47 at a 7% yield. After a sharp sell-off, its yield is now 9%. What has happened to its modified duration?
options: It is still 12.47, because duration is fixed at issue
It has risen, because the bond is now riskier after the fall
It has fallen, to about 10.69, because higher yields make distant cash flows count for less
It has fallen to exactly zero, because the price is below par
body.explanation: At higher yields, the distant coupons and principal are discounted more heavily, so they make up a smaller share of the price and the bond's value is centred earlier. Modified duration falls to about 10.69. Each further 1% rise now costs about 10.7% rather than 12.5%, which is exactly why the price curve flattens on the right.

children.text: Convexity Works in the Bondholder's Favour

Because the actual price curve sits above the duration line on both sides, an ordinary bond gains more than duration predicts when yields fall and loses less than duration predicts when yields rise. Look at the 300 basis point rows: the bond gains 52.14% if yields fall but loses only 28.39% if they rise by the same amount. For the holder, that asymmetry is a free benefit. It is also why, for the same duration and yield, investors will pay a little more for a bond with more convexity.

body.title: What Duration Alone Tells You vs What Actually Happens

columns.label: Duration estimate
points: Treats gains and losses as mirror images
Assumes sensitivity stays the same as yields move
Overstates the loss when yields rise
Understates the gain when yields fall

columns.label: Actual price, with convexity
points: Gains exceed losses for equal yield moves
Sensitivity falls as yields rise, grows as yields fall
Losses are cushioned in a sell-off
Gains are amplified in a rally

body.text: The convexity cushion belongs to the holder of an ordinary bond. If you are on the other side, for example a bank or treasury that has effectively sold long bonds through a hedge or a swap, convexity works against you: your losses in a rally exceed what duration predicts. And as Chapter 2 showed, callable bonds such as many bank Tier 2 and AT1 bonds can have negative convexity near their call price, where gains are capped but losses are not. Lesson 3 of this chapter covers that case.

body.title: Name the gap
body.textWithBlank: The gap between a bond's actual price curve and the straight-line estimate from modified duration is explained by ___.
body.explanation: Convexity measures the curvature of the price-yield relationship. The next lesson turns it into a number you can add to the duration estimate to correct it.

body.title: The maths intuition behind the square

children.text: Any smooth curve can be approximated near a point by a series of terms: a straight-line term that depends on the change, then a bending term that depends on the change squared, then smaller terms after that. For bonds, modified duration supplies the straight-line term and convexity supplies the squared term. Because the squared term grows with the square of the yield change, it is negligible for a 10 basis point move (0.001² is tiny) and substantial for a 300 basis point move (0.03² is 900 times larger). That is the whole reason the error table above grows the way it does.

content.latex: \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx \underbrace{-D_{\text{Mod}} \times \Delta y}_{\text{duration: straight line}} \; + \; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2} \times C \times (\Delta y)^2}_{\text{convexity: the bend}}
content.caption: C is the convexity measure, calculated in the next lesson. Because (Δy)² is always positive, the convexity term always adds to the estimate for an ordinary bond, whether yields rise or fall.

body.title: Nikhil's stress test
body.scenario: Nikhil Shah manages a family office in Ahmedabad. It holds ₹5 crore of an illustrative 30-year 7% G-Sec bought at par, with a modified duration of 12.47. The family's investment committee asks him to stress test the position for a 2013-style shock, and then some: an immediate 300 basis point rise in yields. Nikhil multiplies duration by the move and reports a potential loss of ₹1.87 crore. A committee member also asks what the position would gain in a 300 basis point rally.
body.prompt: Using the table in this lesson, work out the actual loss and gain, explain how far off the duration-only answers are, and tell Nikhil what this means for how he reports risk.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Duration-only estimate for +300 bps: −12.47 × 3 = −37.42%, or about ₹1.87 crore on ₹5 crore.
2. Actual change at +300 bps: −28.39%, a loss of about ₹1.42 crore. Duration overstates the loss by about ₹45 lakh.
3. Duration-only estimate for −300 bps: +37.42%, or about ₹1.87 crore. Actual change: +52.14%, a gain of about ₹2.61 crore. Duration understates the gain by about ₹74 lakh.
4. So the position is far more asymmetric than the duration number suggests: a 300 bp rally is worth nearly twice as much as a 300 bp sell-off costs.
5. For reporting: (a) for small daily moves, PV01 and duration remain the right tools; (b) for stress tests of 100 bps or more, he should either reprice the bond fully at the stressed yield or add a convexity adjustment, covered in the next lesson; (c) overstating the loss is conservative, which is not a disaster, but it can lead the committee to cut a position it could safely hold; (d) he should also stress different moves for different maturities, since a real shock rarely moves every yield by the same amount.

points: The price-yield relationship is a curve. Modified duration is a straight line touching it at today's yield.
For small moves the two agree; for large moves the actual price always sits above the duration line for an ordinary bond.
The error grows roughly with the square of the yield move: about 0.3% at ±50 bps but 9% to 15% at ±300 bps for a 30-year G-Sec.
The curve bends because duration itself changes: the 30-year G-Sec's modified duration is 15.57 at 4% but 9.89 at 10%.
Convexity means gains beat losses for equal yield moves, a benefit to the holder of an ordinary bond.
Use duration for everyday moves, and add convexity or fully reprice for large shocks like the 2013 taper tantrum.
